title: TSMC CEO Hints Company Could Step In If Intel Cannot Meet Customers’ Advanced Packaging Demand - Stocktwits
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) CEO C.C. Wei hinted during the company’s earnings call that the chipmaker could step in if customers struggle to secure enough advanced-packaging supply from Intel (INTC). The remarks came after Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan asked whether TSMC would support customers that initially chose Intel’s EMIB-T packaging technology but later faced supply constraints, according to the Koyfin transcript of the company’s third-quarter (Q3) earnings call. “I try to avoid answering it directly, but let me say that, yes, we will be,” Wei said. “Number one priority I already indicated is that TSMC’s customer’s product can be introduced into the market smoothly. That’s a number one priority. Okay? And that gives you enough of a hint.” TSM stock fell nearly 4% in morning trade amid broader market weakness as concerns around AI spending and hotter-than-expected producer prices weighed on markets. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment behind the chip supplier to companies like Nvidia (NVDA) and Apple (AAPL), improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. Platform data showed a 666% increase in chatter in the same time period. Intel’s EMIB-T and TSMC’s Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) are competing approaches to advanced packaging that connect chip components and high-bandwidth memory into integrated systems used in AI computing. A shortage of packaging capacity can delay deliveries even when the underlying chips are available. Should that happen, clients can either delay their launch or switch to a different supplier. During Intel’s second-quarter (Q2) earnings call in July, CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated that  EMIB-T orders were growing and yield and reliability targets were being met, with the company preparing to scale production to support customers’ 2027 ramps. INTC stock fell over 5% in morning trade on Thursday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the company continued to trend in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day. Wei said TSMC is already producing packages five times the standard reticle size, with plans to expand to nine times and eventually 14 times that size. “We are in the real-world production of 5x reticle size. I don’t believe that anybody can do that today except at TSMC, and the yield is excellent,” he said. “So our customers are very satisfied with the result.” Wei added that the company is also working to reduce packaging costs, stating that its CoWoS technology remains customers’ preferred option. TSM stock fell in morning trade on Thursday despite reporting a Q3 earnings and revenue beat. Earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.91, according to Koyfin, beating Wall Street expectations of $0.89 per share. Revenue rose 50% year-over-year to $46.12 billion, beating analysts’ forecast of $45.69 billion. This was the company’s sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings. It forecast fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue would rise as much as 61% as compared to a year ago. TSM stock has gained over 36% this year. It’s currently trading around 14% below its record high of over $487 seen earlier this month. Microsoft (MSFT) is drawing fresh analyst attention on Thursday ahead of its upcoming earnings report, with four firms raising their price targets on the stock. According to The Fly, TD Cowen, Mizuho, Citi and UBS raised their Microsoft price targets, citing Azure trends, cloud demand and enterprise AI adoption. MSFT stock traded nearly 0.5% higher at the time of writing. According to The Fly, TD Cowen raised its price target on Microsoft to $625 from $540 and maintained a ‘Buy’ rating. The firm updated its model ahead of quarterly results, seeing the potential for a “higher than normal” beat on Azure as the third-party data it tracks screened strongest in history, alongside a full quarter of Fairwater and a bullish read on an OpenAI growth inflection. Mizuho analyst Gregg Moskowitz raised the firm’s price target to $600 from $510 and maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating. Moskowitz said Mizuho’s channel checks in Q3 were “very healthy overall,” with strong public cloud and consumption data points and AI adoption remaining robust. Citi analyst Tyler Radke raised the firm’s price target to $636 from $600 and maintained a ‘Buy’ rating, according to The Fly. Citi said its recent chief investment officer survey and reseller checks reinforced its view that Microsoft’s core productivity and public cloud franchise should accelerate as enterprises increase AI spending. The analyst also considers Microsoft among the best-positioned AI vendors. Meanwhile, UBS analyst Karl Keirstead raised the price target on the stock to $675 from $525 and maintained a ‘Buy’ rating. He said the stock’s 39% rally had raised growth expectations, but Azure and Microsoft 365 fundamentals supported the optimism and the valuation remained reasonable. Separately, UMass Memorial Health announced a multi-year initiative with Microsoft and Accenture (ACN) to modernize its data platform using Microsoft Azure. The unified platform is intended to replace siloed reporting systems and support more advanced analytics. The initiative will also move UMass Memorial’s electronic health record to Azure, connecting clinical, operational and research data on one platform. The health system aims to use the connected data to advance quality and safety goals, including reducing patient length of stay and caregivers’ administrative burden. Accenture will introduce agentic AI tools to automate complex workflows and uncover insights. UMass Memorial Health expects the transformation to improve speed, quality and security while lowering long-term infrastructure costs. SpaceX (SPCX) continued to increase its foothold in the commercial aviation market, with United Airlines (UAL) announcing that Starlink satellite internet service is now available on nearly half of the carrier’s daily flights. The development comes just a week after American Airlines (AAL) announced plans to equip its entire mainline fleet with Starlink. SPCX shares were down about 4% at the time of writing, tracking weakness in the broader space and the tech sector. UAL stock edged marginally higher. United Airlines said Starlink is now installed on more than 635 aircraft. According to a July SEC filing by United, the airline operates 1,579 mainline and regional aircraft. United is adding Starlink to about 20 planes per week and expects to complete installations by the end of 2027. United also launched a Starlink Tracker, allowing travelers to check whether their flights offer the service. Last week, American Airlines announced plans to install Starlink on more than 1,030 aircraft. Installations are expected to begin in early 2027, covering both narrowbody and widebody aircraft. Starlink is also available in 38% of Alaska Air Group’s (ALK) fleet. Alaska Air operates Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. Globally, Qatar Airways already offers Starlink Wi-Fi on 150 widebody aircraft, while Air France is targeting a fleetwide rollout by year-end. Emirates is also set to launch the service. Starlink has also been in the news since SpaceX announced a deal last week to acquire Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz wireless spectrum portfolio. The deal would see SpaceX expand its Starlink Mobile service by combining satellite connectivity with ground-based mobile networks, potentially increasing competition with traditional telecom operators. Intuit (INTU) is expanding its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities with a deal to acquire Sequence, a startup that automates billing, contracts and revenue recognition for businesses. The acquisition, announced Thursday, will add new capabilities to QuickBooks Online Advanced and Intuit Enterprise Suite as the company looks to capture a larger share of the mid-market financial software business. Financial terms were not disclosed.At the time of this writing, INTU stock traded up more than 4%. Sequence's platform automates the quote-to-revenue process, covering everything from pricing and customer contracts to invoicing, collections and revenue recognition. Its AI agents are designed to take over routine finance tasks. The acquisition comes as usage-based and hybrid pricing models create additional work for finance teams, which must track customer contracts, changing consumption and revenue recognition across multiple systems. “Revenue management has long been the most fragmented workflow in the back office,” said Sequence Co-Founder and CEO Riya Grover. The deal would allow Intuit to bring those capabilities into its existing financial software products rather than leaving customers to manage revenue processes across separate applications. Intuit has been investing in AI-powered financial tools to attract businesses with more complex accounting needs. In August, the company expanded its Intuit Intelligence platform across QuickBooks Online Advanced and Intuit Enterprise Suite, introducing conversational AI tools that help finance teams analyze business data, identify discrepancies and automate accounting workflows. The latest acquisition would extend that automation beyond bookkeeping and reporting into the revenue cycle itself. The mid-market push comes against a backdrop of growing business software revenue. Intuit's Global Business Solutions revenue increased 16% year over year to $12.9 billion in fiscal 2026. At its September investor day, the company reaffirmed its fiscal 2027 companywide revenue guidance of $23.28 billion to $23.51 billion, representing 9% to 10% growth. Intuit also expects Global Business Solutions revenue of $13.07 billion to $13.16 billion under its revised reporting structure, which excludes Mailchimp. Apollo Global Management (APO) Chief Economist Torsten Slok stated that the Federal Reserve faces a difficult policy choice as producer prices accelerate and consumers begin pulling back on spending, raising the risk of an uncomfortable mix of persistent inflation and slowing economic growth. “This is a definition of stagflation,” Slok said during a CNBC interview. “We have higher prices, and in response to higher prices, we buy less.” His comments came after U.S. producer price inflation accelerated sharply in August, defying expectations for a decline. The annual producer price index (PPI) rose to 6.3%, its second-highest level in four years, higher than the expected 5.5%. Monthly headline PPI climbed 1.3%, more than double the 0.6% increase economists had expected. Core PPI also exceeded expectations, with the monthly reading coming in at 0.7% against an estimate of 0.3%. U.S. equities traded lower ahead of the PPI data release. After markets opened, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were on track to hit their worst week since June. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was down 0.4%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) dropped 1.3%. Meanwhile, SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) stayed in the green, with gains of around 0.44%. SPY and QQQ were among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Retail sentiment around QQQ  shifted to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day, while chatter increased to’high’ from ‘normal’ levels. According to Slok, the hotter inflation reading complicates the Fed’s efforts to balance price stability against the risk of slowing growth. Slok said policymakers must decide whether to prioritize rising inflation or signs that consumers are beginning to rein in spending. “The challenge for the Fed is: Should they be focusing on inflation going up, or should they be focusing on the slowdown in consumers’ money and the risk of GDP growth?” he said. Slok pointed to housing and autos as early examples of interest-rate-sensitive sectors responding to tighter financial conditions. Mortgage rates have climbed substantially from their pandemic-era lows, while financing and leasing a car have become more expensive. “The more interest rate-sensitive parts of the economy are beginning to respond,” Slok said. “We’re seeing that in housing. We’re seeing that in autos.” He added that consumers are also showing early signs of adjusting their spending as higher prices squeeze household budgets. Slok also warned that the U.S. economy has become increasingly dependent on AI investment, leaving growth vulnerable if companies slow spending on data centers and related infrastructure. “GDP growth is normally two [percent], and now roughly one percentage point of GDP is coming from the AI spending boom,” he said. A slowdown in the build-out could weigh on economic growth even without triggering a recession. The key question, Slok said, is whether the financial returns from AI investment arrive as quickly as investors expect. “What if that payoff does not arrive with the speed that the consensus was expecting?” he said. Slok expects some moderation in data center construction as expectations for earnings and investment returns adjust, but does not anticipate a recession. “I think the answer is that we will not get a recession, but I do think we’ll get some more dampening of the data center build-out,” he said. With PPI inflation at its second-highest level in four years, CME FedWatch data put the odds of a Fed rate hike at 27.1% in October. Penske Automotive Group (PAG) shares rallied around 8% in premarket trading on Thursday after the company agreed to be taken private by Penske Corporation and Mitsui & Co. in a deal valuing the company at approximately $16.3 billion. Roger Penske, chair and CEO of Penske Automotive Group, called the transaction “an important next chapter for PAG,” saying the company would work with Mitsui to build on its operational excellence, drive innovation and expand its business through new opportunities and collaborative projects. Under the agreement, PAG shareholders will receive $212 per share in cash, excluding Penske Corporation, Mitsui & Co. and other members of the investor group. The offer represents an 8.84% premium to PAG’s closing price on Oct. 14, the last trading day before the deal was announced. The deal will be carried out through Motown Acquisition Corp., an entity owned by Penske Corporation and Mitsui. Upon completion, Penske will own approximately 64% of the privately held company, while Mitsui will hold the remaining 36%. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and shareholder votes. Approval requires a majority of outstanding shares entitled to vote, as well as a majority of votes cast by unaffiliated shareholders. Once the transaction closes, PAG shares will no longer trade on the New York Stock Exchange. Penske Automotive is set to report its third-quarter results before the market opens on Oct. 28. Analysts tracked by Fiscal AI expect revenue of $8.39 billion and earnings per share of $3.46. Separately, Penske Automotive’s board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $1.46 per share, up $0.02, or 1.4%, from the previous payout. The dividend represents an annualized rate of $5.84 per share and is payable on Dec. 1 to shareholders of record on Nov. 13, 2026. content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. shares fell 0.2% in premarket trading on Monday amid a broader market sell-off linked to the fresh U.S.-Iran escalation, taking the sheen off the company’s robust June and second-quarter sales update. Revenue in the April-June period came in at NT$1.27 trillion ($39.62 billion), based on Reuters calculations, beating the LSEG/Reuters estimate of NT$1.264 trillion. June sales rose 37% to NT$401.26 billion. The company will release its full results and outlook on Thursday. TSMC makes cutting-edge semiconductors for the likes of Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and components for Apple. The biggest buyers of those chips – including cloud companies Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft – have set aside $725 billion for AI-related investments this year. The latest performance shows steady demand for advanced chips, which power data centers and other systems that power AI applications, smartphones and automobiles. In April, the Taiwanese giant raised its full-year sales guidance and said its capital spending should trend toward the upper end of an existing forecast range of up to $56 billion in 2026. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced in May that the U.S. chip designer would set up a headquarters in Taiwan and invest up to $150 billion annually in the region. Still, TSMC CEO C.C. Wei had warned in June that his company won’t be able to meet demand from American customers for years, even as more manufacturing capacity comes online in the U.S. over the next few years. TSMC stock has gained 43% year-to-date, pushing the chipmaker’s market capitalization above $2 trillion for the first time last month. Late Sunday, HIMS published an Instagram carousel explaining what peptides are, why they have attracted biohackers and how they could become part of mainstream healthcare. The campaign comes as investors search for Hims’ next major growth engine beyond compounded GLP-1 drugs, and as regulators prepare to decide whether seven popular peptides should receive a clearer pathway into the U.S. compounding market. Shares of Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN) and Oracle Corp. The firms covered under the new framework are Microsoft Ireland Operations, Google Cloud EMEA, Amazon Web Services EMEA, and Oracle Corporation UK. Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will jointly oversee the critical services the four companies provide to the financial sector. The aim is to reduce the risk of widespread disruption if a major cloud provider experiences operational issues. Regulatory oversight will apply only to the financial sector, not to their broader business operations. The designated companies will be required to maintain strong systems to identify, manage, and recover from disruptions affecting services used by financial institutions. Regulators will also be allowed to gather information, assess operational resilience, and, when necessary, introduce or enforce CTP-specific rules to ensure the continuity of critical services. “These designations will help ensure the critical services financial firms rely on remain resilient, protecting consumers and businesses while supporting growth across the economy,” said Rachel Blake, Economic Secretary to the Treasury of the United Kingdom. The Critical Third Parties designation was established under the UK’s Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 to improve operational resilience after growing concerns that disruptions at major cloud providers could affect multiple financial institutions simultaneously. The framework builds on the Bank of England’s 2021 assessment that the financial sector’s increasing reliance on a small number of cloud providers warranted stronger regulatory oversight to safeguard essential financial services relied upon by millions of consumers and businesses. Overseas Fab Margin Dilution: Expected closer to 2% for full year 2026; expected to widen to 3% to 4% in the next few years. Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Signs with ACXIF. Third quarter revenue increased 16.2% sequentially to $46.7 billion, exceeding the high end of guidance, driven by strong demand for leading-edge process technologies. Advanced technologies (7nm and below) accounted for 79% of wafer revenue, with 2nm contributing 8%, 3nm 33%, 5nm 28%, and 7nm 10%, demonstrating technology leadership. HPC platform revenue grew 22% quarter-over-quarter, representing 68% of total revenue, fueled by robust AI-related demand. Fourth quarter revenue guidance of $52.3-$54.3 billion implies a 14% sequential increase and 58% year-over-year growth, reflecting continued strong momentum. Full year 2026 revenue growth expected around 44% year-over-year in US dollars, with AI demand extremely robust and no signs of slowdown. Capital budget for 2026 reiterated at $60-$64 billion, with CapEx from 2026 to 2028 expected to be significantly higher than the past three years to support customer growth. N2 technology ramping successfully with good yield, and annual capacity expected to more than double in 2027, supported by smartphone and HPC/AI applications. A14 technology risk production on track for 2027 and volume production in 2028, with more customer activity than N2 at similar stage, indicating strong future demand. Advanced packaging solutions are highly competitive, with 5x reticle size in volume production and development for 9x and 14x reticle sizes underway. Commitment to sustainable and steadily increasing cash dividend per share on both annual and quarterly basis, returning value to shareholders. Gross margin decreased 1.3 percentage points sequentially to 66.4% in Q3 2026, primarily due to margin dilution from the initial ramp-up of 2nm technology. Fourth quarter gross margin guided to decrease further to 66% at the midpoint, due to continued margin dilution from steep 2nm ramp and overseas fabs. Overseas fab margin dilution expected to widen to 3-4% in the next few years, up from closer to 2% in 2026, impacting overall profitability. Consumer and price-sensitive end market segments are being challenged by rising component prices and economic uncertainties, leading to prudent business planning for 2027. Tool supply is tight, and tool price inflation is real, which could increase capital expenditures and pressure costs. Capital intensity remains high, with CapEx significantly higher than past three years, and no dramatic increase in profitability expected overnight. High NA EUV adoption planned for 2030, later than some competitors, potentially raising concerns about technology leadership timing. Power supply situation is a consideration factor in capacity planning, though currently assessed as manageable. AI demand calculation uses a narrow definition excluding CPUs, so the full extent of AI-related demand may not be fully captured in reported figures. Pricing strategy is strategic and varies by market segment, location, and technology, with US production costs higher than Taiwan, potentially affecting margins. Q: Laura Chen of Citi asked how TSMC views the AI revenue CAGR given aggressive AI semiconductor demand, and how it reconciles customer capacity requirements with concerns over data center power availability, funding, HBM, advanced packaging, and laser tightness.A: Chairman C.C. Wei explained that TSMC runs a sophisticated and disciplined capacity planning process, factoring in CSP CapEx, data center build-out, power supply, and other supply chain components. Based on its assessment, demand still exceeds supply, and TSMC is working hard to narrow the gap. CFO Wendell Huang added that demand is extremely robust with no sign of slowdown, and the AI accelerator CAGR will probably be higher than the previously guided mid- to high 50s percentage from 2024 to 2029. Q: Gokul Hariharan of JPMorgan asked whether wafer supply tightness in 2027 could be even greater than in 2026, and whether TSMC's wafer capacity growth could approach or exceed 10% in the next couple of years.A: C.C. Wei said demand is extremely robust and getting higher, with TSMC checking data center build-out and customer demand from multiple angles. The gap between demand and supply remains quite big, and TSMC is putting all its strength into increasing capacity. Wendell Huang added it is too early to discuss capacity increase percentages, but advanced nodes are the main driver of capacity growth. Q: Gokul Hariharan of JPMorgan also asked about TSMC's more aggressive overseas expansion, including potential new fab clusters in Texas and engagement with a customer's Terafab project.A: C.C. Wei confirmed TSMC is expanding in the US because most large customers are there and the US government is helpful. TSMC has evaluated locations outside Arizona, including Texas, and is in discussions with a customer about potentially utilizing Terafab capacity. He emphasized that any such fab must be run by TSMC, and more details will be shared once discussions conclude. Q: Krish Sankar of TD Cowen asked about a secondary wafer market where customers pass wafer allocation to others, and whether TSMC allows this practice.A: C.C. Wei stated this is not a new strategy and TSMC does not allow customers to sublet or auction off capacity. In certain cases, customers can collaborate through mask licensing agreements, but this is not common practice and the amount is very small. Q: Krish Sankar of TD Cowen also asked whether adopting High NA EUV later than competitors, around 2030, puts TSMC at a competitive disadvantage.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC always evaluates new tools for best technology, reasonable cost, and maturity. TSMC plans to use High NA in 2030 when it believes the tool will be mature and cost-effective, and is working with ASML on a 12-inch photomask by 2031. He emphasized TSMC remains confident it is still the best company to offer the most advanced technology to customers. Q: Charlie Chan of Morgan Stanley asked about an IDM customer spending aggressively on capacity and whether A14 could still be a bigger node than N2 despite potential insourcing.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC treats every customer fairly, whether IDM or fabless, and takes internal customer capacity into consideration. TSMC has seen more customer activity for A14 than for 2-nanometer so far and expects A14 to be a bigger node than N2. He declined to comment on specific customer outsourcing plans but guaranteed TSMC takes everything into consideration. Q: Charlie Chan of Morgan Stanley also asked about advanced packaging, including whether TSMC's SoW 3.5D can catch customers moving to larger reticle sizes like 14x, and whether TSMC would support customers if they cannot get sufficient capacity from a competitor's EMIB-T solution.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC's advanced packaging technology is very competitive, with the top priority being to help customers' products reach the market smoothly with best technology and enough capacity. TSMC is in real-world production of 5x reticle size with excellent yield, working on 9x and moving to 14x reticle size. CoWoS remains the number one choice for customers, and TSMC remains very competitive. Q: Sunny Lin of UBS asked how to think about CapEx beyond 2026, including whether CapEx could grow faster than or in line with sales, and whether tool price inflation is a meaningful variable for 2027 CapEx.A: Wendell Huang said it is too early to share CapEx numbers beyond this year, but TSMC has strong conviction in the AI megatrend, and CapEx from 2026 to 2028 is expected to be significantly higher than the past three years. Tool price inflation is real, but the majority of CapEx is related to long-term demand. He added that if TSMC does its job right, revenue growth will outpace CapEx growth. Q: Sunny Lin of UBS also asked about the wider 3% to 4% overseas margin dilution starting in 2027, and whether Arizona expansion is being accelerated.A: Wendell Huang said TSMC is doing everything it can to increase capacity and accelerating everywhere, including in the US. The 3 to 4 percentage point margin dilution from overseas fabs in the latter part of the five-year period remains the case. Q: Haas Liu of Bank of America asked about potential shifts in AI demand mix toward more efficient compute solutions, including agentic AI CPUs and networking switches, and the incremental opportunity for TSMC's manufacturing and packaging business.A: C.C. Wei said AI demand is extremely robust, whether from accelerators or CPUs, and TSMC has seen demand from agentic AI CPUs continue to increase. In TSMC's judgment, demand is still far above its ability to supply, and TSMC is working hard to narrow the gap. Q: Haas Liu of Bank of America also asked whether supporting both conventional power delivery and super power rail technology at future nodes makes the yield learning curve more challenging and impacts gross margins.A: C.C. Wei said the situation is different from previous years, with strong demand from both smartphone and AI HPC applications, and smaller die sizes and large accelerator die sizes happening at the same time. This is to TSMC's advantage because it has been prepared for this, results are excellent, and customers are very happy. He was responding to Mach33 founder and CEO Aaron Burnett, who urged investors to study SpaceX while others were still catching up. Burnett’s post discussed Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas’ observation that few clients appeared to own the stock. In an excerpt shared by Tesla investor and influencer Sawyer Merritt, Jonas recalled asking 40 clients whether anyone owned SPCX shares. “Not a single hand went up,” he said. Jonas argued that assessing SpaceX solely through telecommunications, aerospace and defense, or AI misses the connections between its businesses. “Valuing SPCX is more of an ‘and’ problem than an ‘or’ problem,” he said. “The unusual dimensionality that makes it challenging to value the stock, in and of itself, gives the stock its value.” Burnett questioned why the “loudest” voices on asset pricing often had done the “least work” to understand underlying value, while acknowledging a place for both valuation shortcuts and technical research. “SpaceX is among the most difficult technology suites in the world to ‘intuit’ and getting more complex not less,” he said. “The complexity is equally a challenge and opportunity, depends on your perspective.” Wells Fargo said SpaceX is redeploying engineers from its launch and connectivity divisions to orbital data center work, prioritizing AI satellites ahead of a demonstration launch targeted for the second quarter of 2027. A fully loaded Starship could deliver about 20 times the bandwidth of a Falcon 9 launch carrying V2 Minis, ARK said. The bigger opportunity rests on full reusability, which ARK estimates could cut launch costs to $100 per kilogram or less at scale and make orbital data centers economically feasible. Frontier-model AI could represent more than 90% of SpaceX’s stated $28.5 trillion addressable market, the firm said. “A successful upper-stage catch would put full reusability—and a new era of launch economics—within reach,” ARK said. Federal energy officials announced a conditional $4.2 billion loan commitment Monday to modernize and boost power production across nuclear generation facilities in Pennsylvania and Ohio, targeting rising regional electricity costs and surging energy demand. The funding, extended by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing to Texas-based utility operator Vistra (VST), aims to expand generation capacity across existing facilities without necessitating new power transmission infrastructure. According to department officials, the initiative supports executive measures to bolster domestic nuclear infrastructure and restore American energy output. The planned upgrades focus on Vistra’s Beaver Valley plant in Pennsylvania, along with the Davis-Besse and Perry facilities in Ohio. By executing thermodynamic and hardware uprates, the project will add 433 megawatts of power capacity while maintaining nearly 4 gigawatts of steady baseload electricity—enough to supply power to more than 3 million households. Earlier in January this year, Meta Platforms (META) struck 20-year agreements to buy power from Vistra’s Perry and Davis-Besse plants in Ohio and Beaver Valley plant in Pennsylvania. Beyond expanding immediate output, the modernization strategy will help extend operational life cycles at the three Midwestern plants by up to 20 years beyond their current licensing terms. The conditional loan arrangement also leaves open an option to fund future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak facility in Texas. Construction, engineering, and specialized maintenance during scheduled outage periods are projected to support about 3,000 temporary jobs while protecting thousands of permanent operational positions at the facilities. By boosting generation within established facility footprints, the funding addresses growing power consumption across the 13-state PJM Interconnection grid, which serves major industrial and residential centers throughout the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions. Final disbursement of the $4.2 billion loan remains contingent on Vistra meeting mandatory environmental, legal, technical, and financial criteria required by federal regulators. title: Chip Leader TSMC Delivers Beat-And-Raise Third-Quarter Report - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Meta, SpaceX Earnings Loom After S&P 500, Nasdaq Break Support Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) on Thursday beat estimates for the third quarter and guided above views for the current period. But TSM stock fell after the report. The world's largest contract chipmaker, better known as TSMC, earned $4.60 per U.S. share on sales of $46.72 billion in the September quarter. Analysts polled by FactSet had expected TSMC to earn $4.46 a share on sales of $45.67 billion. On a year-over-year basis, TSMC earnings rose 61% while sales climbed 44%. In local currency, TSMC earnings increased 69% year over year in Q3 while sales rose 51%. For the current quarter, TSMC expects revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. The midpoint of $53.3 billion beat the consensus estimate of $50.22 billion. In the fourth quarter last year, Taiwan Semiconductor posted sales of $33.14 billion. One slight blemish on the quarter was TSMC's softening profit margins. TSMC's gross margin in the third quarter was 66.4%. It was 67.7% in the second quarter. For the fourth quarter, TSMC forecast a gross margin of 65% to 67%, or 66% at the midpoint. On the stock market today, TSM stock slid 1.8% to 422.25 amid the ongoing AI rout. TSM stock has tumbled since hitting an all-time high of 487.47 on Oct. 5. That occurred on the same day as its short-term breakout from a cup base with a buy point of 479, according to IBD MarketSurge charts. Chip stocks have been poor performers of late. The Philadelphia semiconductor index, known as SOX, fell for the seventh straight trading session on Thursday. It closed below its 50-day moving average line on Wednesday. The SOX, which includes the 30 largest chip stocks traded in the U.S., has fallen 12.4% since its Oct. 6 close. TSMC makes chips for a host of fabless chip designers including AMD (AMD), Apple (AAPL) and Nvidia (NVDA). Lately it has benefitted from high demand for chips for data centers running artificial intelligence applications. In the third quarter, shipments of 2-nanometer chips accounted for 8% of TSMC's total wafer revenue. Shipments of 3-nanometer chips accounted for 33% of revenue. Further, 5-nanometer chips accounted for 28% of wafer revenue and 7-nanometer accounted for 10%. Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and smaller node sizes, accounted for 79% of the company's total wafer revenue. "Our business in the third quarter was supported by strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies," Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang said in a news release. "Moving into fourth quarter 2026, we expect our business to be supported by continued strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies, including the steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer technology." TSMC maintained its 2026 capital expenditures budget at $60 billion to $64 billion, with 2026-to-2028 capex expected to be significantly higher than the prior three years. The higher spending reflects the need to increase production capacity to meet continued strong demand for AI chips. TSMC is building 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan over the next several years and another five to six fabs overseas, Wedbush Securities analyst Matt Bryson said in a client note. He maintained his outperform rating on TSM stock and increased his price target on the company's Taiwan-traded shares. At least four equity analysts raised their price targets on TSM stock after the company's earnings report. "Management's tone was emphatically constructive: agentic AI is broadening silicon demand beyond accelerators into CPUs (central processing units) and networking, customers keep raising their requirements and demand still runs ahead of supply," Freedom Broker analyst Egor Tolmachev said in a client note. Tolmachev kept his buy rating on TSM stock and raised his price target to 560 from 475. Needham analyst Charles Shi reiterated his buy rating on TSM stock and raised his price target to 560 from 530. "TSMC reported strong results for Q3 with revenue above the high end of the guidance, and guided Q4 well ahead of the Street," Shi said in a client note. "We are increasing our 2027 and 2028 estimates. We expect 2027 is likely a banner year for TSMC in terms of reaching record revenue and sustaining high growth." Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE:TSM) reported record third-quarter earnings on Thursday, exceeding market expectations as strong demand for advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence continued to support revenue growth. The world's largest contract chipmaker also confirmed that it was considering additional manufacturing facilities in the United States, including potential locations in Texas, as it seeks to expand production capacity. Net profit increased nearly 69% year-on-year to NT$763.06 billion ($23.55 billion) in the three months ended 30 September, exceeding the NT$746.3 billion consensus estimate based on Reuters/LSEG data. Revenue rose 50% to NT$1.49 trillion, reflecting continued demand for advanced chips from AI infrastructure providers and other technology customers. TSMC reported a gross margin of 66.4%, an operating margin of 58.7% and a net profit margin of 51.1%. The results marked the company's sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings and its eleventh consecutive quarter of growth. TSMC is evaluating further manufacturing investment in the United States as demand for advanced semiconductor production continues to increase. During the company's post-results webcast, Chief Executive C.C. Wei confirmed that TSMC had examined potential locations beyond its existing manufacturing operations in Arizona. "We're working very hard to increase our capacity in the U.S.," Wei said in response to an analyst's question. He added that Texas was among the locations being considered for additional facilities. Discussions remain ongoing regarding the structure of any new operations, including whether TSMC would develop and operate the facilities independently or collaborate with external partners. One potential arrangement mentioned involved Elon Musk's Terafab semiconductor manufacturing initiative. No final decision on the location, ownership structure or timetable for additional facilities was disclosed. The possible expansion forms part of TSMC's broader effort to increase production capacity as demand for advanced computing chips continues to exceed existing supply capabilities. Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang warned that TSMC's manufacturing expansion would continue to affect profitability margins as the company invests in additional capacity in Taiwan and overseas. Huang estimated that capacity expansion would dilute gross margins by approximately two percentage points in 2026. He also indicated that the impact from overseas manufacturing facilities could become more pronounced in subsequent years. For the fourth quarter, TSMC expects its gross margin to decline by at least 0.4 percentage points. The company anticipates substantially higher investment requirements in the coming years as it responds to continued demand from artificial intelligence customers. Huang said capital expenditure would be "significantly higher" in future periods, reflecting the need to increase semiconductor manufacturing capacity. TSMC maintained its 2026 capital expenditure budget of between $60 billion and $65 billion. However, Huang did not provide a specific forecast for how much additional production capacity the company expects to bring online over the coming months. The spending plans illustrate the financial commitments required to support demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing, even as higher investment costs create pressure on near-term margins. TSMC expects revenue of between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion for the forthcoming reporting period, representing approximately 58% year-on-year growth, according to the company's guidance. Chief Executive C.C. Wei separately forecast that full-year 2026 revenue would increase by approximately 44% in US dollar terms. The projections reflect continued demand for advanced chips used in artificial intelligence computing, data centres and related applications. "The AI market continues to be very strong… we observe increasing AI demand, fueled by the increasing adoption of agentic AI," Wei said. He also highlighted the growing importance of semiconductor technology within the wider artificial intelligence industry. "The value of semiconductors in the global AI chain is expected to continue to increase," Wei added. The company's outlook suggests that investment in advanced AI systems remains an important driver of semiconductor demand despite broader concerns about technology sector valuations. TSMC's advanced manufacturing technologies continued to account for a significant proportion of its wafer revenue during the third quarter. The company reported that chips manufactured using its 2-nanometre process represented 8% of total wafer revenue. Its 3-nanometre technology accounted for a further 33%. These advanced production processes are used to manufacture high-performance semiconductors for applications requiring substantial computing power and improved energy efficiency. TSMC's manufacturing capabilities have positioned it as a major supplier to companies developing advanced AI processors. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) remains among its largest customers, reflecting the importance of TSMC's manufacturing capacity to the global AI computing industry. The company's results are closely monitored as an indicator of semiconductor demand across the wider technology sector. Its latest earnings followed strong results from semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML Holding (EU:ASML), which also reported continued demand associated with artificial intelligence earlier in the week. TSMC's results came during a period of considerable pressure on semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related equity valuations. Technology stocks have faced selling pressure as stronger US inflation figures increased expectations of further Federal Reserve interest rate rises. Higher borrowing costs have raised concerns about the financial implications of the substantial infrastructure investment required to support AI development. The market reaction has been particularly significant for companies relying heavily on debt to finance data centres, computing infrastructure and other expansion projects. Against that backdrop, TSMC's earnings demonstrated continued demand for advanced semiconductor production, although its own expansion programme is expected to weigh on margins. For investors, the company's ability to increase manufacturing capacity while managing capital expenditure and profitability will remain an important consideration as AI-related demand continues to grow. Operator, can we move to the next participant, please? Next one, Haas Liu, Bank of America. Go ahead, please. Yes. Hi, C.C., Wendell, and Jeff. Thanks for taking my questions, and congrats on the great results. My first question would be on your view regarding the potential shift in AI demand mix. You mentioned in the prepared remarks that the AI accelerator chipset demand is proliferating into agentic AI demand, including CPUs and networking switches. We understand the overall AI investment is still pretty strong and even trending stronger across the board. Can we get more clarity that are you seeing your customers' demand shifting toward more efficient compute solutions, especially monetization gets more important? How should we think about the incremental opportunity for your manufacturing and packaging business? Thank you. Haas' first question is on the AI-related demand. His question is, are we seeing a shift in the AI-related demand more and more to CPU or networking switches and away from AI accelerators? Any type of comment, yeah. Well, all I can say is AI's demand is extremely robust. Whether it's come from accelerator or is more from the CPU side, it's not for me to make a comment. Although we did see the demand from agentic AI CPUs continue to increase. Yes, that is a trend today. Other than that, everything is very robust. I want to emphasize again, in our judgment, we consider all the parameter, and the demand actually is still far above our capability today to supply. We are working very hard to narrow the gap. That's all I can say. Okay. Thank you. That is very clear. My second question is just regarding the yield learning curve going forward for your dual technology tracks strategy going forward. Historically, I think you have been ramping up the yield of a new node through producing the chipsets with smaller die size and simpler design to improve the learning curve of a new node. But for the future node families supporting both a conventional power delivery for the applications like mobile and consumer applications and Super Power Rail technology for HPC and AI chipsets, would operating two process architectures at the same time make the learning curve more challenging or increase the manufacturing complexity? How should we think about the implication to your gross margins from the yield and also cost control perspective? Thank you. Okay, so Haas' second question is really about ramping a new node, the learning curve of yield and cost, and therefore the implication to gross margin, really, I think is what he is driving at. His question is that in the past a new node is mostly ramped with smaller die size and simpler design. But today we have both the smartphone and also with the AI and HPC applications coming in. Does that increase the complexity of the node process architecture, make the learning curve more challenging or difficult, and therefore the implication to the margin? Well, today's situation actually is a little bit different from previous years. Yes, we now have a very strong demand from smartphone and also AI HPC applications. So the smaller die size per se or the big die size in the accelerator, they happen at the same time. This is to TSMC's advantage, let me say that. Because we are good. We have been prepared for this kind of thing, and happy to working with us. So the learning curve, yes, but we are doing a reasonable job, and so the customer are very happy today. Okay. Thank you. Operator, let's move on to the next participant, please. Hi. I really appreciate management taking my question. I have a question on the power as a gating factor. I want to understand, have the power grid constraint led you reduce your customer forecast in the history? Also, could this tighter and tighter power grid surprise make your customer actually accelerating adoption of your Super Power Rail product for the better performance power? Thank you. Okay. Arthur's first question is about the power supply or electricity supply. Is it a gating factor, and have we seen that lead to a reduction in customers' forecast? On the other side or on the other hand, with the tighter power electricity supply, have we seen more customers adoption of Super Power Rail technologies? Well, let me update that. Definitely power supply situation is one of the consideration factor that we are looking into. That's why also we do one more step to double check whether the power supply situation in the U.S. And we have done all the study, and so far so good, let me say that. Whether this kind of situation change our customers' behavior and move more into the backside power rail? Answer is no. Whether you use the backside power, those kind of metallization scheme is based on your need for your product. Okay? Some of the accelerator might be using it, some of the product like mobile phones, they don't use it. So it depends on customer's product. Did I answer the question? Yeah. Thanks. Yes. So just recall the previous discussion on the agentic AI demand on the CPU. So I wonder, according to our previous framework, demand forecast framework, the mid to high 50s growth including the CPU or not, and if we heard our clients increase the CPU forecast significantly, when is the next time we refresh our AI demand growth numbers? Okay. So Arthur's second question is on our, we already stated, but anyway, our AI accelerator definition. He wants to know with the emergence of agentic AI and CPU, does that AI accelerator definition include CPUs or not, and when we will provide inclusion for him. Let me answer the question. It is not included in our AI demands calculation. The reason is very simple, because we cannot identify which CPU user in the conventional server CPU or AI server CPU. Also, it depends on our customer's application and their own allocation. So, no. So far today, we stick to our initial very narrow definition on the AI's demand. Understand. If we have seen a very strong CPU-driven demand, when will we revise up the- Arthur, I think we already said very clearly it is not part of the AI accelerator definition. It is a narrow definition, but it is certainly part of our business. Okay? Okay. Operator, in the interest of time, can we take question from the last participant on the line, please? Yes. Sahej Singh, Stifel Financial. Go ahead, please. Hello. Thank you for the question. Into 2027, you have N3 turning accretive, and now that is crossed over. N2 is still in its diluted ramp, and the overseas dilution is widening. On the offset side, there have been reports of significant price increases across your mature and advanced nodes. Could you provide some color into perhaps some of that conversation? Where pricing does move, does it typically apply across the existing contracted book, or is it mainly being applied to incremental capacity above what customers have already committed to? Yeah. Okay. The first question is, I guess you are asking about the potential puts and takes for next year, or you are asking specifically on pricing? Sorry. For pricing. Okay. It is a very specific question that there are reports that we are increasing the price. He wants to know, does it apply across the existing contracted commitments from customers, or is it mainly for the incremental capacity? Well, we have discussed this kind of thing before, that our pricing strategy is very strategic. It also depends on the market segment, depends on the location, and depends on the technology and something. Once we offer the flexibility of the physical location, like in the U.S., it will be a little bit different from the one we produce in Taiwan. No matter what, we try to get our value to be recognized, and we will give our shareholders the maximum value of our technologies. Understood. Thank you. For the second question, something you said in your prepared remarks which stuck out to me was, we will not be leaving food on the table. Earlier, I think it was maybe one or two weeks ago, there was the announcement via GlobalFoundries that they would be providing silicon interposers to TSMC. I would love some color into how are you thinking through these strategic decisions in terms of procuring from some of the specialty foundries versus providing in-house. Thank you. Okay. His second question is, again, he notes that recently we had an announcement with GlobalFoundries on interposers. How do we view these partnerships, and what is our approach strategically? Well, let me answer the question. We designed a deal with GlobalFoundries, and this is part of our overall strategy in the back-end supply. Actually, our number one priority is to help our customer to be successful in their market. We want them to be fully supported by all the supply, including the front end and back end. Definitely, we have a little bit shortage on the back end, and we would like to work with our so-called partner with GlobalFoundries so that both TSMC and GlobalFoundries can support TSMC's customer for their product to be introduced with enough support on the capacity. Okay. Thank you for your questions. Thank you for all the participants. This does conclude our question-and-answer session. Before we conclude today's conference, please be advised that the replay of the conference will be accessible within 30 minutes from now. The transcript will become available 24 hours from now, and you can find both will be available through TSMC's website at www.tsmc.com. Again, thank you for joining us today. We hope everyone continues to stay well. Have a good autumn, and we hope you will join us again next quarter. Thank you and have a good day. title: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom - CNBC
content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips. Here are TSMC’s third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate: The world’s largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier. TSMC’s third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company’s earnings call. The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand. TSMC’s stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company’s elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email. TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process. Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC’s careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems. “Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity,” he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers’ ability to deploy the chips they order. Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC’s total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips. By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23%  growth rate. TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors. The company’s free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago. TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain. TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule. TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earnings announcement in July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona. The chipmaker is also reportedly considering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence.
